![CLIP training for one batch of six language-image training examples. Green boxes are positive pairings (we seek to increase their value); these are the six training pairs. Red boxes are negative pairings (we seek to decrease their value); these are all other possible pairings within the batch. Inspired by figure 1 of \cite{radford2021learning](figures/vision_and_language/clip_training_fig.png){width="85%" #fig-vision_and_language-clip_training}

After training, we have a text encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder
$f_\ell$ that map to the same embedding space. In this space, the angle
between a text embedding and an image embedding will be small if the
text matches the matches. 

:::{.column-margin}
The dot product between
unit vectors is proportional to the angle between the
vectors.
:::


@fig-vision_and_language-clip_mapping_diagram_two_branch shows how a
trained CLIP model maps data to embeddings. This figure is generated in
the same way as @fig-neural_nets-vit_mapping_plot: for each encoder we
reduce dimensionality for visualization using **t-distributed Stochastic
Neighbor Embedding** (**t-SNE**) @tsne. For the image encoder, we show
the visual content using icons to reflect the color and shape depicted
in the image (we previously used the same visualization in @sec-representation_learning-expt_designing_embeddings_with_contrastive_learning).

It's a bit hard to see, but one thing you can notice here is that for
the image encoder, the early layers group images by color and the later
layers group more by shape. The opposite is true for the text encoder.
Why do you think this is? One reason may be that color is a superficial
feature in pixel-space while shape requires processing to extract, but
in text-space, color words and shape words are equally superficial and
easy to group sentences by.




![CLIP @radford2021learning mapping diagram, using the same technique as described in @sec-neural_nets_as_distribution_transformers. To reduce dimensionality we apply t-SNE @tsne separately for the text encoder and the image encoder. Within each encoder, we run t-SNE jointly across all shown layers. ](figures/vision_and_language/clip_mapping_diagram_two_branch.png){width="100%" #fig-vision_and_language-clip_mapping_diagram_two_branch}

After passing the data through these two encoders, the final stage is to
normalize the outputs and compute the alignment between the image and
text embeddings. @fig-vision_and_language-clip_shared_embedding shows
this last step. After normalization, all the embeddings line on the
surface of a hypersphere (the circle in the figure). Notice that the
text descriptions are embedded near the image embeddings (icons) that
match that description. It's not perfect but note that this is partially
due to limitations in the visualization, which projects the
$768$-dimensional CLIP embeddings into a 2D visualization. Here we use
kernel principle component analysis @scholkopf1998nonlinear on the
embeddings, with a cosine kernel, and remove the first principle
component as that component codes for a global offset between the image
embeddings and text embeddings.

interactions.label: Focus Concept
interactions.teaches: Clicking an icon or text label isolates its specific trajectory through the network layers, showing how its relative position changes layer-by-layer up to the joint space.

interactions.label: Clustering Overlay
interactions.teaches: Reveals how early layers in the vision stack group embeddings by simple color features, while later layers transition to grouping by semantic shape — contrasting with text layers which handle both abstractions differently.

demo_steps.title: Two paths to one space
demo_steps.narration: CLIP maps images (left) and text (right) through deep neural networks into a shared joint embedding space (top). Initially, the raw features are represented in entirely different modalities — pixels versus language tokens.

demo_steps.title: Early vision groups by color
demo_steps.narration: In the early layers of the Image Encoder (bottom planes), watch how the clusters form around simple pixel colors. Toggle the 'By Color' overlay: the pink circle and pink square cluster together because low-level color dominates early ViT representations.

demo_steps.title: Late vision extracts shape
demo_steps.narration: By the final ViT layers (top planes), representations rearrange completely. Toggle 'By Shape': the pink circle now clusters with the blue circle and red circle. The network has successfully abstracted 'circularity' from raw color.

demo_steps.title: Tracing a concept to alignment
demo_steps.narration: Click on the 'blue triangle' concept. Watch both its image representation and its text label trace their distinct paths upward. At the very top, their normalized vectors land close together on the hypersphere, enabling zero-shot retrieval.

phase2Evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several highly functional and pedagogically useful interactions: (1) A 'Focus' dropdown to isolate individual concept trajectories across the vision/text stacks; (2) A 'Clusters' overlay dropdown that reveals color grouping in early layers and shape grouping in late layers; (3) Interactive clicks on the 3D nodes, trajectories, and HTML text labels themselves to focus concepts dynamically; (4) Interactive proxies on the left encoder, right encoder, and joint embedding space that trigger contextual narrations matching the planned demo steps. This delivers an outstanding, highly integrated multi-modal interactive experience.
phase2Evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concepts: (1) CLIP's multi-layered encoder mapping showing how early image encoder layers group representations by color while late layers group by shape. (2) Alignment of different modalities into a single joint embedding space. Both concepts are accurately represented and interactively taught. The 'Visualization Mode' dropdown lets the user overlay color clusters on the early layer (L0) and shape clusters on the late layer (L4), which directly illustrates the text's assertion ('early layers group images by color and the later layers group more by shape'). Tracing a single concept (e.g. 'blue triangle') shows how both the icon and the phrase project upward through their respective stacks into the joint embedding sphere, representing the shared modality constraint.
phase2Evaluation.notes: The implementation is exceptionally high quality, achieving perfect scores in both conceptual accuracy and interactivity. It beautifully illustrates CLIP's multi-modal alignment with highly functional features like interactive node filtering, early/late layer clustering overlays, and contextual narrations.

evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several highly functional and pedagogically useful interactions: (1) A 'Focus' dropdown to isolate individual concept trajectories across the vision/text stacks; (2) A 'Clusters' overlay dropdown that reveals color grouping in early layers and shape grouping in late layers; (3) Interactive clicks on the 3D nodes, trajectories, and HTML text labels themselves to focus concepts dynamically; (4) Interactive proxies on the left encoder, right encoder, and joint embedding space that trigger contextual narrations matching the planned demo steps. This delivers an outstanding, highly integrated multi-modal interactive experience.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concepts: (1) CLIP's multi-layered encoder mapping showing how early image encoder layers group representations by color while late layers group by shape. (2) Alignment of different modalities into a single joint embedding space. Both concepts are accurately represented and interactively taught. The 'Visualization Mode' dropdown lets the user overlay color clusters on the early layer (L0) and shape clusters on the late layer (L4), which directly illustrates the text's assertion ('early layers group images by color and the later layers group more by shape'). Tracing a single concept (e.g. 'blue triangle') shows how both the icon and the phrase project upward through their respective stacks into the joint embedding sphere, representing the shared modality constraint.
evaluation.notes: The implementation is exceptionally high quality, achieving perfect scores in both conceptual accuracy and interactivity. It beautifully illustrates CLIP's multi-modal alignment with highly functional features like interactive node filtering, early/late layer clustering overlays, and contextual narrations.
